x: Weight is the force with which the Earth attracts a body. Tides, free-fall acceleration and orbital motion are other effects of gravity, not weight.
t: Discriminate weight from the other effects of gravity.

x: Option C is incorrect: the Earth is not perfectly spherical but slightly oblate, bulging at the equator because of rotation and gravity.
t: Check each statement for an absolute word like "perfectly".

x: Gravity holds gases near the planet, an effect called atmosphere retention. Tides and orbits are separate effects of gravity.
t: Recall each named effect of gravity.

x: Both are true and R explains A: free-fall acceleration g does not depend on mass, so all bodies fall together in a vacuum.
t: Check whether R is the reason for A.

x: Acceleration due to gravity always points towards the centre of the Earth, which is why things fall straight down.
t: Recall gravity as a centre-directed pull.

x: I, II and IV are correct: g is greatest at the poles, falls with height and is slightly reduced by rotation. III is false because g decreases with depth, becoming zero at the centre.
t: Check how g changes with latitude, height, depth and rotation.

x: Weight is mass times gravitational acceleration, W = mg, so it is measured in newtons.
t: Recall W = mg from F = ma.

x: Both are true: mass is a scalar measure of matter that stays constant, while weight is a vector force that varies with g from place to place.
t: Discriminate mass (constant scalar) from weight (variable vector).

x: Both are true and R explains A: the poles lie closer to the Earth's centre and have no centrifugal effect, so g and weight are highest there.
t: Check whether R gives the cause of A.

x: Three are linked to zero weight: the Earth's centre, very great height and a freely falling lift. At the poles weight is maximum.
t: Discriminate where g falls to zero from where it peaks.

x: Both are true and R explains A: satellite and astronaut fall towards the Earth with the same g, so there is no normal force and the astronaut feels weightless.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Free fall makes the normal force zero, an orbiting satellite and astronaut fall with the same g, true g is zero at the centre, and zero effective gravity means apparent weight N = 0, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Discriminate true zero gravity from apparent weightlessness.

x: Zero-g training uses aircraft flying parabolic paths, which give astronauts short spells of free fall.
t: Recall how weightlessness is simulated on Earth.

x: All three are correct: astronauts in space stations are in continuous free fall, microgravity is used to study fluids, crystals and physiology, and satellite instruments are built for weightlessness.
t: Recall the uses and effects of microgravity.

x: Low Earth Orbit spans about 160–2000 km; the ISS sits near 400 km. About 36,000 km is geostationary orbit, a trap.
t: Discriminate LEO altitude from geostationary altitude.

x: LEO is 160–2000 km, geostationary is about 36,000 km above the equator with a 24-hour period, polar orbits pass over the poles and elliptical orbits have unequal apogee and perigee, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the defining feature of each orbit type.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the circular-orbit condition is centripetal force equal to gravity, while apogee and perigee describe elliptical orbits.
t: Check whether R is about the same thing as A.

x: Weight is the Earth's pull on a body, gravity keeps planets in orbit, tides come from the Moon and Sun's differential pull, and gravity retains the atmosphere, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall each effect of gravity.

x: The ISS orbits at about 400 km, inside Low Earth Orbit. 36,000 km is geostationary height.
t: Recall ISS altitude as a LEO value.

x: Both are true: far from the Earth g and weight approach zero, and satellite instruments are designed to work in weightlessness.
t: Recall how g falls with distance from the Earth.

x: Weight is greatest at the Earth's surface; it falls going up, going down and in far space, and is zero at the Earth's centre.
t: Recall that g peaks at the surface.

x: All three are correct: weight is in newtons, mass is in kilograms, and weight can vanish in weightlessness while mass stays the same.
t: Discriminate mass from weight.

x: All four reduce weight: height above the surface, depth below it, the Moon (about one-sixth) and far space where it nears zero.
t: Recall that weight peaks at the surface and falls elsewhere.

x: Microgravity experiments study human physiology, along with fluid behaviour and crystal growth. The other options are effects of gravity, not research topics.
t: Recall what microgravity research studies.

x: Ignoring air resistance, every freely falling body accelerates at g, about 9.8 m s⁻², whatever its mass.
t: Recall that free-fall acceleration equals g.

x: Of points on the surface, the equator is farthest from the Earth's centre because of the equatorial bulge. Strictly, a point at very large height is farther still, so the question means surface points.
t: Recall the Earth's oblate shape with an equatorial bulge.
